Raising in a regulated category

Strategy · Fintech

In short: fintech investors underwrite trust and durability, not growth alone. Show the licence as an asset, the economics per funded account, the losses and the compliance cost in the model, and the plan for when a partner leaves.

Key points

  • Move licensing from the risks slide to the assets slide, with status, dates, budget and a responsible person.
  • The unit is a funded account; state the sign-up to funded ratio yourself.
  • Show compliance cost and loss rate as separate model lines, with trends and control changes.
  • Answer the partner bank question on one slide, including notice period, concentration and exit plan.
  • Put uncomfortable items, including regulatory correspondence, in the data room on purpose.

This is operating guidance from go-to-market work, not investment, legal or regulatory advice.

Licensing is an asset, price it like one

Most decks bury licensing in "regulatory" on the risks slide. Move it to the assets slide.

A granted licence tells an investor three things. The regulator looked at you and said yes. You can operate without borrowing someone else's permission. And the next competitor needs the same months and the same spend to catch up.

A licence in progress is still an asset if you show the path: the application date, the stage, the known gaps, the budget, the fallback if it slips. Part 3 said raise against evidence, not narrative. A dated application with a named responsible person is evidence.

What you cannot do is leave it vague. "We are exploring licensing options" reads as "we have not started."

The unit is a funded account

Sign-ups are not the unit in fintech. Downloads are not the unit. A verified account with no money in it is a cost, not a customer.

Build the unit economics around the funded account: cost to acquire one, cost to verify and onboard one, revenue per funded account per month, and how long a funded account stays funded. Then the payback period on that basis.

Investors who know the category will convert your sign-up numbers to funded accounts in their heads anyway. Do it for them and show the ratio. A low ratio with a clear plan beats a hidden ratio every time.

Compliance and losses belong in the model

Two lines fintech models often leave out: the cost of compliance and the cost of losses.

Compliance cost is people, tooling, audits, legal, and the verification spend per account. It scales with accounts and with the number of markets. Put it in as its own line so an investor can see it does not eat the margin at scale.

Losses are fraud, chargebacks, credit losses if you lend, and operational errors. Show the rate, the trend, and what you changed when it moved. A loss rate that fell after a control change is a strong slide. A loss rate that is absent is a question you will get asked in a worse setting.

The partner bank question

If you run on a partner bank or a BaaS provider, every experienced fintech investor will ask the same question. What happens if they give notice?

They are not asking whether you have a dependency. Almost everyone does. They are asking whether you understand it. The answers they want:

What they ask What a good answer contains
Who is the partner? Named, with the agreement term and notice period
What do they control? Account issuance, custody, card programme, compliance sign-off, or all of it
What do they cost? Fees in the model, including minimums and step-ups
What is concentrated? Share of revenue or accounts running through that partner
What is the exit plan? Second partner in diligence, or a licence path that removes the dependency, with a timeline

A one-slide version of this table does more for the round than another slide on market size.

The fintech data room

Part 4 said run the round like a sales process, with the data room built before the first meeting. In fintech the room has a specific extra shelf.

Licences and registrations, current and in progress. The compliance programme: policies, the named compliance officer, the monitoring approach, the last audit or review and what it found. Bank partner and BaaS agreements. Any external audit or attestation. Loss data by month with the control changes marked. Complaint volumes and resolution times. Regulatory correspondence, including anything uncomfortable.

The uncomfortable items go in on purpose. Investors find them anyway. Finding them in your room says you run the company; finding them elsewhere says you hide things.

Strategic investors want distribution or data

Banks, payment networks and large payroll or accounting platforms invest in fintech for reasons that are not purely financial. Usually they want one of three things: distribution into your customers, data on a segment they cannot see, or an option to acquire you later.

None of these is bad. All of them change the deal. A strategic investor can bring a partnership that cuts your acquisition cost in half. They can also bring exclusivity terms that close off the other channels in Part 8.

Decide what you want from them before the meeting. Then ask directly what they want from you. The answer tells you whether the cheque is worth the terms.

The checklist

  • [ ] Licensing shown as an asset with status, dates, budget and responsible person
  • [ ] Unit economics built per funded account, with the sign-up to funded ratio stated
  • [ ] Compliance cost and loss rate each appear as their own model line, with trends
  • [ ] One slide answers the partner bank question, including the exit plan
  • [ ] Data room contains licences, compliance programme, partner agreements, audit, loss data and regulatory correspondence
  • [ ] For each strategic investor, you have written what they want and what you want before the first call

Common questions

What do fintech investors look for in a pitch?

Trust and durability, not growth alone: licensing shown as an asset, economics per funded account, compliance cost and losses in the model, and a plan if a partner bank leaves. The article notes it is operating guidance, not investment, legal or regulatory advice.

How should a fintech startup answer the partner bank question from investors?

Name the partner with the agreement term and notice period, what they control and cost, how concentrated you are, and the exit plan: a second partner in diligence or a licence path, with a timeline.

What should be in a fintech data room?

Licences and registrations, the compliance programme, bank partner and BaaS agreements, audits or attestations, monthly loss data with control changes marked, complaint data and regulatory correspondence.

What do strategic investors like banks want from a fintech?

Usually distribution into your customers, data on a segment they cannot see, or an option to acquire you later. Each changes the deal, so decide what you want before the meeting.
